analysis_note: All pre-1900 excerpts are plain-language renderings of public-domain sources.

documents.source_line: Codex Mendoza: tribute list recorded by Mexica scribes under Spanish direction
documents.sourcing_note: Compiled by Aztec scribes for the Spanish king; purpose is to record what conquered provinces owed. The document itself is a product of conquest, but its contents describe the pre-conquest tribute system from the Mexica point of view.
documents.text_or_description: Each year, the province of Tochtepec must deliver: 400 loads of large cloaks, 400 loads of loincloths, 20 lip plugs of gold, jars of honey, and warriors' costumes adorned with bright feathers. Forty provinces pay tribute in this manner to Tenochtitlan.

documents.source_line: Pedro Cieza de León, Spanish chronicler, describing Inca administration in Peru
documents.sourcing_note: A Spaniard who traveled the Andes and interviewed Inca subjects; writing for Spanish readers. His admiration is notable because he served the conquering power yet credits Inca governance.
documents.text_or_description: Along the royal roads the Incas built great storehouses filled with maize, cloth, and weapons. The people labored in turn for the Inca, and from these stores they were fed and clothed in times of famine or war. No one went hungry while the storehouses stood full.

documents.source_line: Florentine Codex: account of Mexica religion given by Nahua elders to the friar Bernardino de Sahagún
documents.sourcing_note: Nahua informants speaking to a Franciscan friar; purpose on their side is to preserve ancestral knowledge, on his to understand it. The account links warfare, religion, and state power from an Indigenous perspective.
documents.text_or_description: The Mexica believed the gods had sacrificed themselves to set the sun in motion. To repay this debt, captives taken in war were offered upon the temples, so that the sun would not cease to move. War and worship were one duty.

documents.source_line: Garcilaso de la Vega, son of an Inca princess and a Spanish conquistador, writing in Spain
documents.sourcing_note: A mestizo author writing for European readers; purpose is to defend Inca civilization against Spanish contempt. His Inca heritage gives him insider knowledge, while his Spanish audience shapes his praise.
documents.text_or_description: The Inca was revered as the son of the Sun, and none might look him in the face. His word was law throughout the four quarters of the empire, and the people obeyed him as a god upon the earth.

documents.source_line: Quipu: knotted cords used by Inca administrators
documents.sourcing_note: A 19th-century illustration of surviving Inca artifacts; purpose is educational. The quipu embodies the Inca method of rule: centralized record-keeping without writing, tracking tribute, census, and storehouse inventories.
documents.text_or_description: Cords of different colors hang from a main rope, each tied with knots in patterns. Inca officials used these quipus to record how much each community owed in labor and goods, and what the storehouses held.

documents.source_line: Map of the Aztec Empire, c. 1519
documents.sourcing_note: A modern historian's map; purpose is to show extent. The pattern of a small core ruling many tributary provinces illustrates the Triple Alliance's method: domination without direct administration.
documents.text_or_description: The map shows the island capital Tenochtitlan at the center of a compact empire in central Mexico, surrounded by tributary provinces that paid goods but kept their own rulers.

documents.source_line: Map of the Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu), c. 1525
documents.sourcing_note: A modern historian's map; purpose is to show extent. The empire's vast length along the Andes helps explain Inca methods: roads, storehouses, and resettlement to hold distant regions together.
documents.text_or_description: The map shows the Inca Empire stretching more than 2,500 miles along the Andes, from present-day Ecuador to Chile, divided into four quarters joined by an extensive road network.

prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the extent to which the Aztec and Incan empires used similar methods to consolidate their power in the period c. 1300-1500.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: argue methods were similar in purpose (extracting surplus, divine legitimation) but different in form (Aztec tribute in goods vs. Inca labor tax; Triple Alliance hegemony vs. direct bureaucracy); corroborate economic control across Docs 1, 2, and 5; qualify similarity by noting the Aztec left local rulers in place while the Inca reorganized populations.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (context: compiled under Spanish rule, describing a Mexica system); Doc 3 (point of view: Nahua elders preserving knowledge for a friar); Doc 4 (purpose: a mestizo author defending Inca civilization to Europeans); Doc 2 (audience: Spanish readers, yet admiring Inca rule).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate both empires within post-classic American state-building: the Aztec rising after the fall of earlier central Mexican powers, the Inca expanding from Cuzco after 1438; both built on earlier Andean and Mesoamerican traditions of tribute and sacred kingship.

evidence.describe: All seven describable; strongest: Docs 1, 2 (economic methods), Docs 3, 4 (ideology), Doc 5 (administration).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the Aztec Triple Alliance (1428) and flower wars; Inca mit'a labor, resettlement (mitmaq), and the royal road system; human sacrifice as Mexica state ritual; ancestor veneration of Inca mummies.
evidence.support: 'Similar' line: Docs 1, 2 (surplus extraction), Docs 3, 4 (divine legitimation), Docs 6, 7 (territorial expansion). 'Different' line: Docs 1 vs. 2 and 5 (goods tribute vs. labor/bureaucracy), Doc 6 vs. 7 (hegemonic vs. administrative control).

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'extent' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

sample_thesis: The Aztec and Inca empires used similar methods to consolidate power to a considerable extent, since both extracted surplus from conquered peoples and legitimized rule through divine kingship; however, their methods differed significantly in form, as the Aztec relied on tribute in goods from semi-independent provinces while the Inca imposed direct bureaucratic control through labor obligations and record-keeping.
title: Aztec and Inca Methods of Rule
